title: Clarence Love's Lounge and learning tunes by ear
summary: Playing blues in B flat, then Clarence Love's Lounge, with Tulsa's big band scene; he learned standards in a year.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well I don’t know if you can remember but you went to this gig with Jimmy “Cry Cry” is that right, and did someone say, “Okay blues in A” or did you just —
No. You just started playing and you heard it. And usually the blues were in B flat. B flat 7. Like a boogie woogie kind of sound.
I love it that years later you’re playing B flat 7 with Pharoah Sanders.

Well it wasn’t too long after this episode with Jimmy “Cry Cry” that what’s his name, it jumped off my tongue, I ended up in the jazz club in Tulsa, Oklahoma, which was called Clarence Love’s Lounge. Clarence Love was one of the big band leaders throughout the 20s and early 30s that traveled throughout the southwest along with another local big band headed by — jumped right out of my head now — but it’ll come back to me — but he apparently had reasonable — well Tulsa is not too far north of Houston, not too far south of Kansas City, right? 92 miles east of Oklahoma City. It was right in the heart of Route 66 so there were a lot of musical activity in that area. So Clarence and Ernie Fields, the other band leader was, they were fashionable throughout the whole southwest, from Kansas City to Dallas to New Mexico. And so when I entered the scene I entered right in the heart of all of that and found myself in Clarence Love’s Lounge where I knew nothing about chord changes. Nothing. But they put me on the stage and said, you know, count off something, we’re playing this tune, and I had to listen to it and play. Because I was the only bass player around. So apparently I had a decent ear because you know after the year that is the complete year of my junior year in high school I knew all my standard tunes. You know I was just, you know, not only did I have a fairly decent ear with Jimmy “Cry Cry” but I had a pretty good placement of that tone being you know, off boogie woogie when I entered Clarence Love’s place which says that I had a respectable feeling about the placement of my quarter notes which would keep the rhythm and the feeling while they played whatever it was, regardless of the notes that I played, that feeling was prevalent. Remember I told you about that?
And by the time I entered college the next year I knew all my standard tunes.

Well the percussive qualities of the stand-up bass I think are so important, beyond the incorrect notes you might play if you were providing that rhythm for the dancers and so forth, that would have been enough to keep you on the bandstand.
There were dancers also. We won’t go into that.
That’s when I grew up quite rapidly as a young man.
